title: Law of Total Probability and Conditional Expectation
objectives: Partition a sample space and apply the law of total probability to mix scenario probabilities
State and apply the law of total expectation E[X] = sum of P(B_i) * E[X | B_i]
Interpret conditional expectation as the best forecast available given information
Blend regime-conditional return distributions into a single unconditional forecast
motivation: Markets do not have one behaviour, they have regimes: calm and volatile, expansion and recession. Risk teams rarely know which regime tomorrow belongs to, but they can estimate each regime's own statistics and the odds of each regime. The law of total probability, and its expectation twin, are the tools that stitch scenario-level knowledge into one unconditional number, the mathematics inside every stress test and blended forecast.

blocks.md: A **partition** is a set of events that are disjoint (only one can happen) and together cover everything (one must happen): bull versus bear market, recession versus growth, system A versus system B handling a request. Partitions earn their keep through the **law of total probability**: the overall chance of an event $A$ is the average of its within-scenario chances, weighted by scenario odds.

blocks.caption: Law of total probability over a partition $B_1, \dots, B_n$

blocks.title: Worked example: blending default probabilities
items: Scenario weights: recession next year with probability 0.2, growth with probability 0.8, a genuine partition.
The blended rate (3.2%) is not any regime's own rate, it is the probability-weighted mixture, which is what an unconditional risk number must be.

blocks.md: Partitions also explain why many market distributions look lumpy. If calm days are $N(0, 0.5^2)$ and turbulent days are $N(0, 2^2)$, the blended distribution is **not** normal, it has a sharp peak in the middle from the calm regime and heavy shoulders from the turbulent one. Every regime-switching model in production is the law of total probability applied to whole distributions, not just to means. The rule gives you permission to model the parts you understand and let the weighting do the joining.

Expectations obey the same law, and this version does more work in finance than any other line in basic probability. The **conditional expectation** $E[X \mid B]$ is the mean of $X$ computed inside scenario $B$ - the best single-number forecast you can make while knowing the scenario. Averaging those scenario forecasts with scenario probabilities recovers the unconditional mean:

blocks.tex: E[X] = \sum_{i} E[X \mid B_i]\, P(B_i), \qquad E\left[E[X \mid Y]\right] = E[X]
blocks.caption: Law of total expectation (tower rule)

blocks.title: Worked example: regime-blended daily return
items: Model (hypothetical): bull regime with probability 0.3, mean daily return $+2\%$; bear regime with probability 0.7, mean $-1\%$.
So the blended average daily return is $-0.1\%$ even though the bull regime is positive, the regime you are *more likely* to be in dominates the average.

Reading: $E[r \mid \text{bull}] = 2\%$ is the forecast once you know the regime; $E[r]$ is the honest forecast before you know. Mixing up the two is how desks end up quoting bullish numbers to everyone.

blocks.md: The compact statement $E[E[X \mid Y]] = E[X]$ is called the **tower property**: first forecast within each slice of information, then average the forecasts over the information you actually have. A 2x2 joint table makes it concrete. Let $Y$ = regime and let $X$ = 1 if a signal fires, 0 otherwise, with joint probabilities:

blocks.title: Verifying the tower property on the table
items: Average the forecasts by regime odds: $0.46 \times 0.6087 + 0.54 \times 0.2222 = 0.28 + 0.12 = 0.40$.
Direct computation: $E[X] = P(X = 1) = 0.40$ - the two routes agree, as the tower property promises.

blocks.caption: Simulate regime-conditional returns: the overall sample mean settles near -0.1%, the probability-weighted blend of the two regime means.

blocks.title: Scenario blending and VaR
blocks.md: A VaR model that ignores regimes answers the wrong question. Total-expectation logic says: compute the loss distribution *inside* each scenario, then mix with scenario probabilities. Stress testing is the same machinery with the weights flipped, put probability 1 on the recession scenario and read the conditional tail. Conditional expectation is also the first step toward Expected Shortfall, the average loss given that you are in the tail.

blocks.code:
p_bull, r_bull, r_bear = 0.3, 0.02, -0.01
e_r = p_bull * r_bull + (1 - p_bull) * r_bear
print(round(e_r, 4))

# tower property on the 2x2 signal table
p_bull_ = 0.46
print(round(p_bull_ * (0.28 / 0.46) + (1 - p_bull_) * (0.12 / 0.54), 4))
blocks.caption: Both routes to the unconditional number: blending means, and averaging conditional forecasts.

guidedExercise.prompt: An insurer has two policy segments: retail (80% of policies, claim probability 0.02 per year) and commercial (20%, claim probability 0.06). (a) Compute the overall probability that a policy claims in a year. (b) The average claim size is \$50,000, use total expectation to compute the expected claim cost per policy per year.
hints: (a) Retail vs commercial form a partition, weight each segment's claim probability by its share.
(b) E[cost] = E[cost | claim] * P(claim), here every claim costs the same amount.
guidedExercise.solution: (a) $P(\text{claim}) = 0.8 \times 0.02 + 0.2 \times 0.06 = 0.016 + 0.012 = 0.028$. (b) $E[\text{cost}] = P(\text{claim}) \times 50{,}000 = 0.028 \times 50{,}000 = \$1{,}400$ per policy per year, the number the premium must exceed.

independentExercise.prompt: Within the bull regime, the daily return is +3% or +1% with equal probability; within the bear regime it is +1% or -3% with equal probability. Regime odds are 0.3 bull / 0.7 bear. Compute $E[r \mid \text{bull}]$, $E[r \mid \text{bear}]$ and the unconditional $E[r]$.
hints: First reduce each regime to its own mean, that is conditional expectation.
Then blend the two regime means with the regime probabilities.
independentExercise.solution: $E[r \mid \text{bull}] = 0.5 \times 0.03 + 0.5 \times 0.01 = 0.02$ ($+2\%$). $E[r \mid \text{bear}] = 0.5 \times 0.01 + 0.5 \times (-0.03) = -0.01$ ($-1\%$). $E[r] = 0.3 \times 0.02 + 0.7 \times (-0.01) = 0.006 - 0.007 = -0.001$ ($-0.1\%$). You could also average over all four joint outcomes, the tower property guarantees the same answer.

commonMistakes: Using overlapping scenarios in the total-probability sum, the cases must be disjoint and exhaustive.
Quoting a conditional mean (e.g. bull-regime +2%) as the unconditional forecast.
Averaging conditional means with equal weights instead of the correct scenario probabilities.
Confusing E[E[X | Y]] = E[X] with the claim that E[X | Y] is a constant, it is a random variable, one forecast per scenario.
realWorldApplication: Weather services, insurers and reliability engineers all forecast by scenario: compute each weather regime's own number, then publish the probability-weighted blend. It is the only defensible way to average over uncertainty you cannot remove.
quantFinanceApplication: Multi-regime VaR models compute tail risk within each market regime and blend by regime probabilities; stress testing re-runs the same calculation with probability forced onto one regime. Expected Shortfall, the average loss conditional on being in the tail, is a conditional expectation, and is the metric regulators prefer over VaR.
summary: A partition is a set of disjoint, exhaustive scenarios; the law of total probability averages event probabilities across it.
Total expectation: $E[X] = \sum_i E[X \mid B_i] P(B_i)$ - scenario means blended by scenario odds.
Tower property: $E[E[X \mid Y]] = E[X]$; forecast within each slice, then average the forecasts.
Conditional expectation $E[X \mid B]$ is the best point forecast given the information 'B happened'.
Regime models, stress tests and expected shortfall are all this one idea wearing different clothes.

quiz.prompt: Recession occurs with probability 0.2 (default rate 0.08 within it) and growth with probability 0.8 (default rate 0.02). What is the overall default probability?
Which statement is the tower property?
options: $E[X \mid Y] = E[X]$ for every value of Y
$E[X \mid Y] \ge E[X]$ whenever Y carries information
$E[E[X \mid Y]] = E[X]$ - averaging conditional forecasts over Y recovers the unconditional mean
quiz.explanation: The tower property says a two-stage forecast (within scenario, then across scenarios) equals the direct unconditional mean. Option 2 would mean information is useless, false in general; options 3 and 4 are not identities at all.

quiz.prompt: Bull regime (probability 0.3) has mean daily return +2%; bear regime (probability 0.7) has mean -1%. Compute the unconditional mean daily return (decimal, e.g. -0.001).
What does this Python code print?
quiz.code:
p_bull, r_bull, r_bear = 0.3, 0.02, -0.01
e_r = p_bull * r_bull + (1 - p_bull) * r_bear
print(round(e_r, 4))

quiz.prompt: For a partition $B_1, \dots, B_n$ to be usable in the law of total probability, it must satisfy:
options: The $B_i$ must be independent of the event A
The $B_i$ are pairwise disjoint and their union is the whole sample space
quiz.explanation: The scenarios must cover every possibility exactly once, disjoint and exhaustive. Equal weights or independence are not required; unequal regime odds are the normal case.

quiz.prompt: Explain in one or two sentences why $E[r \mid \text{bull}]$ can be positive while $E[r]$ is negative.
quiz.modelAnswer: The conditional mean only describes the bull slice of outcomes. The unconditional mean weights each slice by its probability, so a frequently-occurring negative regime (0.7 weight) can outweigh a rarely-occurring positive one.
quiz.explanation: Total expectation blends conditional means with scenario probabilities; here $0.3 \times (+2\%) + 0.7 \times (-1\%) = -0.1\%$. The conditional number answers a different question than the unconditional one.

flashcards.back: $P(A) = \sum_i P(A \mid B_i) P(B_i)$ over a disjoint, exhaustive partition $B_1, \dots, B_n$.
$E[X] = \sum_i E[X \mid B_i] P(B_i)$; compactly $E[E[X \mid Y]] = E[X]$.
$E[X \mid B]$ is the best single-number prediction of X given that B occurred, the mean recomputed inside scenario B.
Same machinery: blended forecast mixes scenario results by probability; a stress test forces probability 1 onto one scenario and reads the conditional result.
